narration: Some of the richest people alive drive old cars, wear the same gray T-shirt every day, and eat fast food for breakfast. They live like they're almost normal.
Meanwhile, on paper, many of them barely seem to earn anything at all. Some report less taxable income than a schoolteacher. And that is not an accident.

memeTop: can't be taxed on your income
memeBottom: if you never take an income
narration: Because there's a strange trick at the heart of modern wealth: the richer you are, the less you may need to officially 'earn.'
One investigation found the twenty-five richest Americans paid a real tax rate, measured against their growing wealth, of only about three percent.
The average worker, whose wages are taxed before they even hit the bank account, pays a far higher share. So how does that happen — legally?
And a worker can't play the same game. Your salary is reported, withheld, and taxed before it reaches you — there is nowhere for it to hide.
Let's run the numbers on why the rich work so hard to look like they're not.
heading: Why the Rich Pretend to Be Poor

narration: The whole thing rests on one distinction that most of us blur together every day: the difference between income and wealth.
You already know this at a small scale. Someone can own a paid-off house worth two million dollars and still earn a modest salary. Asset-rich, income-modest — same idea, smaller numbers.
Income is the money that flows to you in a given period — a salary, a wage, the cash arriving this month.
Wealth is different. Your net worth is the current value of your assets, minus your debts — everything you own that has value.
Here's the key: our tax system is built mostly to tax income — the flow. It is very bad at taxing wealth — the pile that just sits there, quietly growing.
And the rich are not income-rich. They're asset-rich. Their fortune is a mountain of stock and property — while the salary they actually report can be almost nothing.
caption: tiny income, a mountain of assets

narration: So picture the two numbers side by side. The income a billionaire reports can be almost nothing. The wealth they hold can be beyond imagining.
So step one of looking poor is simply: don't take a big salary. Many founders famously pay themselves one dollar a year.
The one-dollar salary is almost a Silicon Valley tradition. Founders of Google, Oracle, and more have all done it. It signals humility — and it minimizes taxable income.

label: MARK ZUCKERBERG
caption: salary: $1 a year
narration: Mark Zuckerberg takes a salary of one dollar. So does the head of more than one giant company. On an income tax form, a dollar is almost nothing to tax.

label: JEFF BEZOS
caption: fortune lives in Amazon stock
narration: Jeff Bezos built one of the largest fortunes on Earth, almost all of it in Amazon shares — not in a giant salary he had to pay tax on each year.

label: ELON MUSK
caption: paid in stock, not salary
narration: Elon Musk's wealth is overwhelmingly Tesla and SpaceX stock. For years he took essentially no cash salary at all — the shares were always the point.
A one-dollar salary isn't a sacrifice. When nearly all your wealth is stock, your paycheck was never where the money was.
Because the real wealth is in shares they own. And here's the beautiful part, for them: simply owning something that goes up in value is not taxed at all.
A capital gains tax is a tax on the profit realised on the sale of an asset. The key word is 'sale.' No sale, no tax.
So while your stock balloons from a million to a billion, that gain is only on paper. It's an 'unrealized' gain — and the tax man cannot touch it until you sell.
caption: not sold = not taxed

narration: This is how someone becomes a billionaire without ever 'earning' a billion. The company's share price does the heavy lifting — all on paper, all untaxed, until the day they sell.

props.name: chartup
props.label: the share price does the work

narration: Which creates an obvious problem for them. If selling triggers the tax, how do they get cash to actually live on?
The answer is a quiet strategy with a blunt nickname — and it's where the money to live comes from.
heading: Buy, Borrow, Die

narration: Step one: buy. Acquire assets — stocks, companies, real estate — and simply hold them, letting the value grow, untaxed, for decades.
Real estate adds its own magic. On paper, buildings 'lose' value each year through depreciation — creating paper losses that cancel out real income, even as the building actually rises in price.
Step two: borrow. Instead of selling stock and paying tax, they take out loans using that stock as collateral. And a loan is not income — so it isn't taxed.
Banks even sell a product for exactly this: a securities-backed line of credit. Pledge your shares, receive cash to spend, and never sell a single one.
Fund managers get their own door, called carried interest — a quirk that lets a big chunk of their pay be taxed at lower investment rates instead of ordinary income rates.
A billionaire can borrow millions to live on, at tiny interest rates, and legally owe almost nothing in tax on that cash — because borrowed money isn't earnings.
Step three — the grim one: die. When assets pass to heirs, their taxable value is often reset to the current price, in a rule called the stepped-up basis.
A high stepped-up basis can greatly reduce the heir's taxable gain. Decades of growth that was never taxed can effectively be wiped clean on death.
So the ultimate tax shelter is, bluntly, death. A lifetime of untaxed growth can pass to the next generation with the slate wiped nearly clean.
Put it together — buy, borrow, die — and you get a way to live like a king for a lifetime, pass on a fortune, and pay startlingly little tax along the way.
caption: buy, borrow, die

narration: Crucially, most of this is tax avoidance — the legal use of the tax rules to reduce what you owe. It is not the same as illegal tax evasion.
In certain years, reporters found, some of the very richest people legally paid zero dollars in federal income tax — while their fortunes still grew by billions.

memeTop: earn a salary and get taxed
memeBottom: own assets, borrow, and barely get taxed
narration: It's all perfectly legal. The tax code simply treats a mountain of assets very differently from a monthly wage.
But low taxes are only half the story. The other half is a performance — and some of it is completely real.
heading: The Frugal Flex

narration: Because here's the twist: many of the most famous billionaires genuinely do actually live modestly. It isn't all an act.

label: WARREN BUFFETT
caption: ~$149B — still in his 1958 house
narration: Take Warren Buffett, worth over a hundred billion dollars. He still lives in the modest house he bought in 1958, and famously grabs a cheap McDonald's breakfast.
Buffett is one of the best-known investors in the world — and a walking advertisement for spending far, far less than you could.
Buffett has also pledged to give almost all his wealth away. That's genuinely generous — and, not coincidentally, one of the most tax-efficient moves a billionaire can make.

label: SAM WALTON
caption: richest man in America — drove a pickup
narration: Sam Walton, who built Walmart into a giant, drove a battered old pickup truck — even when he was the richest man in America.
That's the frugal flex. Behind a twenty-year-old car and a plain T-shirt sits a fortune most people can't even picture.
caption: …drives a 20-year-old car

label: INGVAR KAMPRAD
caption: IKEA founder — flew economy, old Volvo
narration: Ingvar Kamprad, the founder of IKEA, reportedly flew economy class, drove an old Volvo for years, and furnished his home with — what else — IKEA.

label: STEVE JOBS
caption: Apple salary: $1
narration: Steve Jobs famously took a one-dollar salary at Apple for years. The paycheck was a rounding error; his Apple and Pixar stock was the real fortune.
For some, it's genuine habit — thrift that helped them get rich in the first place. Frugality is simply the avoidance of waste and extravagance.
That's the dictionary definition — the avoidance of waste, extravagance, and lavishness. For some billionaires, it's a sincere value.
But let's be honest — it's also, conveniently, a brilliant strategy. Because looking poor buys a billionaire several very valuable things.
There's even a name for the fashionable version of this now — 'stealth wealth,' or quiet luxury. No loud logos. The flex is that you no longer need to flex at all.
So why would a billionaire actively want to look like they're not? There are at least four reasons.
heading: Why Pretend?

narration: Reason one: taxes and scrutiny. The less visible income you have, and the quieter you are about your wealth, the less attention you attract from tax authorities and the public.
Reason two: envy and safety. Flaunting billions invites resentment, lawsuits, con artists, even kidnapping threats. Blending in is a form of security.
This is a real concern, not just vanity. Visible, flaunted wealth genuinely does attract lawsuits, scams, and security threats to a family. Blending in can be simple self-defense.
Reason three: image. 'Relatable' billionaires get admiration instead of anger. A plain T-shirt is surprisingly good public relations.
Reason four: focus and brand. 'I don't care about money, I care about the mission' is a powerful story — for customers, employees, and investors alike.
And the daily uniform — the hoodie, the gray tee, the black turtleneck — is half convenience and half branding. It quietly says: I'm not doing this for the money.
So the humble image and the low tax bill reinforce each other. One looks like virtue; the other quietly saves a fortune. Both point the same way: look smaller than you are.
Which raises the uncomfortable question — if the rich pay so little, who actually pays?
heading: Who Pays?

narration: The answer is: people whose money is income, not assets. If your wealth is a paycheck, it's fully visible, and it's taxed before you ever see it.
That's the real gap. A nurse or an engineer can easily pay a higher share of their yearly gains than someone worth a thousand times more.
caption: the 'true tax rate'

title: Share of yearly gains paid in tax
narration: Stack it up. A typical worker can hand over roughly a quarter to a third of what they make. The ultra-wealthy, measured against their rising fortune, can pay just a few percent.
This is exactly what investigative journalists uncovered — a nonprofit newsroom obtained tax data showing how little the ultra-wealthy really paid.
The data told a consistent story: the more of your wealth sits in assets rather than wages, the lower your real tax rate tends to fall. It flips what most people assume.

memeTop: the tax code: tax income heavily
memeBottom: the rich: so I'll just have no income
narration: The system taxes what workers have — income — and barely touches what the rich have — assets. It's not a glitch. It's the design.
A billionaire is simply someone whose net worth is at least a thousand million. Notice the word: net worth. Not income.
And it's always been this way. The first billionaire, oil baron John D. Rockefeller, hit the mark back in 1916 — and even then, the fortune was in oil and shares, not a salary.
So what's the lesson hiding inside all of this?
heading: The Lesson

narration: The big one is this: income is a terrible measure of how rich someone truly is. The wealthiest people on Earth can have, on paper, almost no income at all.
So when a headline says someone 'only earned' a modest sum, that may be completely true — and completely beside the point. Watch the assets, not the salary.
So train yourself to ask a different question. Not 'what do they earn?' but 'what do they own, and what is it worth?' That's where the real wealth always hides.

memeBottom: being 'low income' and being poor are not the same thing
narration: Low income and low wealth are two completely different things. The rich have learned to show you the first while quietly keeping the second.
And there's a fair point buried in here too. Taxing assets that only exist on paper is genuinely hard, and can have real side effects. This isn't a simple story of villains.
Some countries have tried a direct wealth tax — an annual levy on net worth itself. Many have quietly dropped it: the wealthy are mobile, and assets are genuinely slippery to value.
But understanding the game changes how you read the world — and your own money. Most ordinary wealth is built the same quiet way: owning assets, not chasing a bigger paycheck.
And the honest takeaway isn't just envy. The same engine works, in miniature, for anyone: real wealth is built by owning assets that grow — not by chasing a slightly bigger paycheck.
So let's total up the trick.
heading: The Final Math
kicker: how to be rich and look poor

narration: Take a tiny salary, so there's little income to tax. Hold assets that grow untaxed. Borrow against them for tax-free cash. And live modestly, so nobody asks questions.
It is, when you see it laid out, almost elegant. The rich aren't really pretending to be poor. They're hiding how the money actually works.
So the next time you see a billionaire in a cheap T-shirt climbing out of an old car, smile — and remember the mountain of quiet, untaxed assets parked just out of frame.
